paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Red and brown seaweeds are highly successful marine organisms that can be found in many shallow seas. Although they have many plant-like features, red and brown seaweeds are not true plants. Like plants, they obtain food by photosynthesis using solar energy, converting this energy into organic matter. But unlike plants, they use pigments other than chlorophyll to trap the sunlight, hence their red and brown colours. There is disagreement among scientists on how to classify them. Some regard red and brown seaweeds as algae (simple photosynthetic organisms) and green seaweeds as plants, others view all seaweeds as algae, there are even some who classify all seaweeds as kinds of plants.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Red and brown seaweeds live in and are supported by water, so they have no need for strong skeletal supports or moisture-retaining tissues. Some seaweeds have stiff stalks, and others have chambers filled with gas, called pneumatophores, that hold up their long leaves towards the light and away from grazing sea-bed animals. Unlike most plants, red and brown seaweeds do not need roots to absorb water and nutrients - they absorb nutrients directly from the water and photosynthesise over their entire surface. Instead of roots, seaweeds have an anchor called a holdfast. Red and brown seaweeds vary enormously in form from a minute single cell to giant kelp which can grow to more than 100m long. Depending on the species, red and brown seaweeds can reproduce asexually by fragmenting or division – where parts of the plant break off and grow into new individuals and sexually by producing spores.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Red and brown seaweeds have evolved to adapt to environments which are often challenging. As well as having to protect themselves from animals hunting for food, seashore and rock pool species need to cope with daily and seasonal extremes of moisture, temperature and salt levels. This is particularly the case on tidal shorelines, where the sea comes in and out on a daily basis. One such adaptation is the fact that certain varieties of brown seaweed have developed a resistance to drying out, so they can live higher up the beach than many other varieties. Although they may dry out at low tide, these species can rapidly absorb seawater and resume photosynthesis as soon as the tide returns. Other seashore brown seaweeds produce mucus, both to protect them from drying out and to deter animals from grazing on them. Some seaweeds are annuals, growing, reproducing and dying within a year. Others have parts which produce new leaves or fronds every year. Some red seaweeds that colonise disturbed areas have even developed two distinct phases during the year. During the calm season they produce long leaves which disappear when the weather turns stormy, leaving a dried-out substance which is resistant to wind but which protects the seaweed, thereby enabling it to grow the following year.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Red and brown seaweeds thrive in fast-moving water on exposed coasts or on current-swept sea beds. In cooler places, they often dominate rocky seashores. There are other varieties which are not attached to the ocean floor. Some of these grow in sheltered lagoons, while others grow in soft mud, anchoring themselves into the mud. Because of light limitations, seaweeds do not usually grow below 30m deep. However, in the clearest waters, such as the Mediterranean, they can grow below 100m. The red seaweeds are better suited to these conditions as they have pigments that enable them to grow in deeper water and cope with darker, shadier conditions. Although most red seaweeds are more suited to cooler conditions, there is one variety, the coralline, which is found in shallow sunny waters with temperatures ranging between 23 and 29 degrees Celsius. Although it grows only 10-30mm a year, it is instrumental in cementing coral reefs and in building other carbonate reefs.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most unusual unattached variety is the brown sargassum or gulfweed, found mainly in the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic Ocean. This species floats at the surface of the open ocean, forming the basis for a unique ecosystem. Due to the specific ocean currents in this region, large mats of yellow-brown sargassum seaweed float on its surface, offering shelter and food for communities of small crustaceans and fish, including freshwater eels. A very specialised organism which relies on the sargassum is the Sargassumfish. This frog-like creature has evolved fins on its chest which can grasp clumps of weed and enable it to scramble around the seaweed mats and hunt for prey. It is also thought that the seaweed mats have an important role in long-distance transport of marine life to isolated islands.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Seaweed not only affects marine life, but also impacts on human lives in many ways. It plays a vital role in economies around the world, particularly in places such as Zanzibar, a series of islands close to Tanzania in Africa. Harvesting the seaweed provides much-needed jobs for the local women here, making them financially independent. The uses of seaweed worldwide are far-reaching – from food production as a fertiliser in farming to its use in gels, cosmetics and pharmaceutical products.
